newsitem.title: USA: Lawyer says Toys "R" Us didn't stop competitors.
newsitem.headline: Lawyer says Toys "R" Us didn't stop competitors.

text.p: A lawyer for Toys "R" Us on Wednesday denied government charges his company suffocated price competition in the sale of Barbie dolls and other playthings, arguing that the nation's largest toy seller faces fierce rivals.

"There has been cutthroat price competition," said Michael Feldberg on the opening day of a trial before an administrative law judge. "Toys "R" Us is a discounter but it does not have the lowest prices -- Wal-mart is the downward price leader."
But government lawyers argue that Toys "R" Us worked with toy manufacturers to freeze out even tougher competitors -- warehouse clubs like Costco that have aggressively cut prices.
"It got to the point where the manufacturers didn't want to offer any products to the clubs without checking with Toys "R" Us," declared Richard Dagen of the Federal Trade Commission.
Lawyers for a handful of large toy manufacturers watched from the audience as the two sides slugged it out in their opening arguments for the trial, expected to last weeks.
More than once, lawyers for toy companies like Mattel Inc. and Hasbro Inc. jumped up to interrupt the opening statements, lest they reveal a company secret.
But those secrets were nothing that might interest children such as, say, research on what might become the next "Tickle Me Elmo."

Instead, the secrets were in more than 80 cardboard file boxes crammed with price records, memoes and other material. So much evidence has been piled into the wood-panelled courtroom that several rows of chairs had to be removed.
Judge James Timony will hold some of the trial in secret so that lawyers can question executives from toy manufacturers and retailers on pricing and market information.

In a skirmish before the main arguments, Timony ruled that employees of Toys "R" Us could not be present during secret sessions when proprietary information from its rivals or suppliers was discussed. Feldberg said he would challenge that ruling in Federal District Court.

During opening arguments, the government alleged that Toys "R" Us organised toy manufacturers to sell the warehouse clubs only "combo packs," which cost more than individual items. Consumers could not make direct price comparisons because they found toys packaged together. For example, Barbie might be packaged with Ken or extra outfits.
But Feldberg countered that warehouse clubs often prefer to sell "combo packs" for all kinds of items, not merely toys.

In any event, he said, only a tiny number of toys were at issue. He said that last year Costco could only point to 13 toys it was unable to obtain, out of more than 74,000 different kinds of toys made.
Feldberg said Toys "R" Us merely let the toy makers know that it "reserved the right not to carry identical items sold by the manufacturer to warehouse clubs."
Lawyers for the government said the end result of the practice by Toys "R" Us was higher prices for consumers.
If the judge finds for the government, it will order Toys "R" Us to "cease and desist" from compromising competition. The ruling can be appealed to the full commission and then to federal courts.
Toys "R" Us' stock rose 87.5 cents to $27.625 on the New York Stock Exchange.
